They attribute the rise to thin domestic buying. The bourse has shown signs of rebounding recently — gaining in 15 out of the past 16 sessions. However, analysts saw little change in market sentiment amid mostly domestic trading as investment funds settled their positions before the end of the year. "This doesn't really look like a rebound to me," an analyst noted. Mainly, there is a bit of domestic buying, and some of the gains may be due to seasonal factors rather than broader market optimism.

author: AlexanderSmith
text: Britain's commercial property market may be improving, but it has not yet reached a clean bill of health, according to a senior Bank of England official. "It would be rash to conclude that the market is now unambiguously healthy in all respects. There are still several factors which will continue to pose challenges to the investment, banking, and valuing communities," said Pen Kent, executive director at the Bank of England. Kent noted that although lease lengths have stabilized temporarily, clauses allowing tenants to break leases are becoming more common.

author: AlexanderSmith
text: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's dispute with suspended star fund manager Nicola Horlick highlights a "merry-go-round" hiring system started by investment banks, according to banking sources on Wednesday. "One of the industry's failings is that it doesn't bring people up through the system. When a firm needs someone, it steals people from a competitor. This creates a destructive merry-go-round which can't be in anyone's interest," one banker said. Newspapers reported that DMG suspended Horlick on Tuesday due to allegations that she attempted to lure colleagues at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, where she was head of UK equities.

author: AlexanderSmith
text: Judith Mayhew, who became the new head of the Corporation of London, stated that the city will defend its share of foreign exchange trading when a single European currency is introduced. "We must maintain our market share at all costs," she said during an interview with Reuters. The Corporation of London is responsible for London's traditional financial hub. Mayhew, a 48-year-old New Zealander who has been living and working in the City of London since 1976, emphasized that the organization will continue playing a crucial role in ensuring that London remains competitive in the global financial markets.

author: AlexanderSmith
text: "Superwoman" fund manager Nicola Horlick announced her resignation on Thursday from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), leaving what she called a feeling of "turmoil" among fund managers at the German-owned bank. A spokesman for Horlick, who had been head of British pension fund business at DMG's Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), told Reuters that she had quit and was planning legal action against her former employer over "constructive dismissal." Horlick had been suspended on Tuesday pending the outcome of an internal investigation into what Deutsche Morgan Grenfell described as "a potential breach" of company policy.

author: BenjaminKangLim
text: Liu Xiaobo, a Chinese dissident, has filed a lawsuit against Beijing authorities for sending him to a labor camp without trial, according to his wife. Liu urged Beijing's Xuanwu District Court to overturn a decision by the Beijing Re-education Through Labor Committee to send him to a labor camp for three years. "I refuse to accept the decision," Liu said in his suit, a copy of which was provided to Reuters. "I am appealing... not out of fear of losing freedom... but to defend my right to free speech."

author: BenjaminKangLim
text: China's propaganda machine on Thursday hailed the selection of Hong Kong's first post-colonial chief executive as the beginning of "true democracy" in the territory. "This is a day to be remembered in Hong Kong's democratic development," the China Daily said of the choice of shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa as chief executive-designate of post-colonial Hong Kong. "It is...the beginning of Hong Kong's true democracy," the official newspaper said in a commentary. Tung was elected on Wednesday by a 400-member Selection Committee -- its members hand-picked by Beijing -- making him the new leader of Hong Kong.

author: BenjaminKangLim
text:
China's Communist Party leader Jiang Zemin urged Taiwan not to create additional barriers, according to reports from major Chinese newspapers on Friday. "Taiwanese authorities must not artificially set up new obstacles," Jiang was quoted as saying on Thursday, just one day after the election of the first post-colonial chief executive of Hong Kong. He did not provide further details.

Hong Kong will return to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, 1997, following 150 years of British rule. Jiang highlighted the importance of maintaining peaceful relations between the two regions during this occasion.

author: BenjaminKangLim
text: China has pledged to open its insurance, stock, retail, wholesale, and banking sectors to foreign investment as part of a drive for long-delayed entry into the World Trade Organization. From 1997-2000, China is expected to open its insurance and stock markets wider to foreign investment, according to a statement from Ma Jixian, an official of the State Economic and Trade Commission under the cabinet. The pledge was included in a unilateral action plan submitted by China to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Philippines last month, as reported by the China Daily.

author: BernardHickey
text: Global media group News Corp Ltd told analysts in a telephone briefing on Thursday that it still expected 20 percent profit growth for the 1996/97 year, despite a below-expected first-half profit result, as reported by analysts. They did say that they were still on track for the 20 percent growth, according to a senior Sydney media analyst who attended the morning teleconference briefing between company officials and U.S. and Australian analysts. Another senior media analyst, who requested anonymity, echoed this statement, saying that News Corp had reiterated its August 1996 forecast of 20 percent profit growth.

author: BernardHickey
text:
Solid growth in the Commonwealth Bank of Australia's (CBA) home loan portfolio has brightened its profit outlook slightly, and this should underpin its half-year result due for release on Wednesday, according to analysts. The bank is expected to report a profit rise of around one percent for the six months ending December 31.

CBA itself has been warning since early 1996 that margin pressure would ensure flat profits for the year to June 30. However, some analysts say CBA has been privately more bullish in recent months. "It's been outlined by"

author: BernardHickey
text: Australia's largest home mortgage lender, the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA), announced a surprisingly strong 11% surge in first-half 1996/97 profits on Wednesday, despite erosion of its interest margins. CBA said good cost control and a 33% surge in business lending more than offset a further squeeze in home loan margins. "Business volumes during the first half of 1996/97 were pleasing, leading to a better-than-expected interim result," CBA managing director David Murray told a news conference. This is likely to lead to a slightly better performance.

author: BernardHickey
text: Analysts said on Wednesday that they would increase their forecasts for the Commonwealth Bank of Australia's (CBA) year net profit by about A$50 million to A$1.15 billion after a surprisingly strong first-half result. CBA posted a net profit for the six months to December 31 of A$602 million, up 11% from A$542 million in the previous comparable half and well above analysts' expectations of A$535 million to A$560 million. However, analysts noted that CBA's announcement of another round of unprompted mortgage rate cuts had dampened their enthusiasm. "I will have"

author: BradDorfman
text: Mercury Finance Co.'s troubles escalated Friday when the company announced it would not be able to pay $17 million in commercial debt that same day. Its stock lost 86% of its value. The auto lender's stock plummeted by $12. 75 to close at $2. 125 on the New York Stock Exchange after its initial trading on Wednesday. It reached as low as $1. 625. Based on more than 172 million shares outstanding as of early November, this drop would have resulted in significant losses for shareholders.

author: BradDorfman
text: Mercury Finance Co.'s agreement to buy a consumer finance business fell through Thursday due to an auto-loan company admitting false accounting led to inflated earnings and firing its chief accountant. Meanwhile, the person responsible for overstating earnings may cooperate with federal authorities. BankBoston Corp. terminated its agreement to sell its Fidelity Acceptance Corp. unit to Mercury for 32. 7 million shares of Mercury stock. When the deal was announced on January 10, the stock was valued at around $458 million. Mercury Finance's stock price is not mentioned in the provided text.

author: BradDorfman
text: Mercury Finance Co.'s troubles escalated Friday when the company announced it would not be able to pay $17 million in commercial debt that same day. Its stock lost nearly 90% of its value, falling from $13 to $1. 875 on the New York Stock Exchange. After opening for trading Friday afternoon for the first time since Tuesday, the stock price dropped to as low as $1. 625. Based on over 172 million shares outstanding as of early November, this means the company faces significant financial difficulties.

author: BradDorfman
text: FBI agents searched the headquarters of troubled Mercury Finance Co. on Monday, following news of accounting issues leading to overstated earnings. The company announced changes in leadership, naming turnaround and bankruptcy specialist William Brandt Jr. as president and CEO. Brandt replaces John Brincat, who resigned but remains employed and part of the board. FBI agents, carrying a search warrant, arrived late Monday morning at Mercury's headquarters.

author: DarrenSchuettler
text: Bre-X Minerals Ltd. said Wednesday that it would consider merger offers at the right price, but was content for now to develop Busang - the richest gold discovery this century - with its existing partners. "The 'For Sale' sign is not on the front yard," Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh told analysts in a conference call. "That is not to rule out discussions with a potential suitor if the price is right. The old expression 'everything has its price' must be taken into account here." His comments came after an agreement was reached.

author: DarrenSchuettler
text:
Canadian police announced that they anticipate additional charges stemming from an ongoing sex abuse scandal involving young boys at Maple Leaf Gardens, the famous home of the Toronto Maple Leafs hockey club. Police have identified at least a dozen new victims of a former Gardens employee who was charged this week with alleged sexual abuse of a teenage boy nearly two decades ago.

Gordon Stuckless, a former backstage helper for concerts and hockey games, is scheduled to appear in a Toronto court on Tuesday to face charges of indecent assault and gross indecency.

author: DarrenSchuettler
text:
Canadians are experiencing a winter of dismay as their national religion—ice hockey—is shaken by sex scandals, fraud trials, and the decline of their once-dominant teams. This year marks the 25th anniversary of Canada’s greatest triumph on ice—a last-minute victory in a series against the Soviet Union that whipped this placid country into a patriotic frenzy.

"It was the one time that we were distinctly Canadian," said Paul Henderson, a journeyman player who achieved hockey sainthood for scoring the winning goal in the final game.

author: DarrenSchuettler
text: A monster shake-up of Canada's biggest city, Toronto, has sparked a citizens' revolt against Ontario's ruling Conservatives, raising eyebrows among those who do business in the country's financial capital. This clean, peaceful city — sometimes called "New York run by the Swiss" — recently became a battleground in the so-called "Common Sense Revolution," initiated by Ontario's Conservative Premier, Mike Harris. Harris promises leaner, cheaper government, aiming to merge Toronto and six neighboring municipalities into a single "megacity" of 2.4 million people. The new city would house approximately 800, 000 residents.

author: DavidLawder
text:
Ford Motor Co., following several competitors in offering "certified" used cars, announced Monday that its Ford and Lincoln brands are starting used vehicle warranty programs that will eventually be available nationwide. Under these programs, Ford and Lincoln-Mercury dealers will undergo special inspections and reconditioning processes and offer factory-backed warranties and three-day, money-back guarantees.

"This is not just an individual, dealer program," said Ford division spokesman Dan Bedore. "It's backed by the Ford Motor Company." The Ford Division program will be launched in the spring after a regional rollout.

author: DavidLawder
text: The Canadian Auto Workers union's choice of Chrysler Corp as its strike target on Wednesday sets up a battle between General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co to determine which company will lead bargaining talks with the larger United Auto Workers. Currently, Ford appears to be gaining an edge, according to analysts. Detroit's second-largest automaker, previously considered unlikely to be targeted by the UAW, recently offered concessions aimed at addressing the contentious issue of outsourcing, analysts say. "Ford is working hard," one analyst commented.

author: DavidLawder
text: General Motors Corp. announced on Thursday that it anticipates an $870 million decrease in its fourth-quarter earnings due to recent strikes in the United States and Canada as well as costs related to its new United Auto Workers contract. In its quarterly 10-K report submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission in Washington, D.C., the automobile giant highlighted that its Delco Electronics division experienced a substantial drop in future profit margins following price reductions and the loss of GM-related business. GM pointed out that the expenses linked to the U.S. and Canadian strikes were incurred.

author: DavidLawder
text: The man accused of a shooting rampage at a Ford Motor Co. plant that left one person dead and three others injured was reportedly depressed over a rejection of a marriage proposal by a woman who worked at the factory, authorities said Friday. Gerald Atkins, 29, a former U.S. Army paratrooper, planned an elaborate escape from the car assembly plant in Wixom, Michigan, leaving a backpack in nearby woods that contained fresh clothing, water, and military food rations. Atkins was arraigned on more than two dozen criminal charges Friday, including those related to the shooting incident.

author: EdnaFernandes
text: Anglo-U.S. auto-components-to-aerospace giant LucasVarity said on Tuesday that it is evaluating some takeover offers for the 13 companies slated for disposal as part of its post-merger corporate shake-up. Victor Rice, CEO, told Reuters that the company expects to engage in active negotiations regarding the sale of some of these non-core units shortly. Only eight of the 13 businesses listed for sale were mentioned in the restructuring statement released earlier. Rice stated that major businesses such as aerospace and electronics were not included among the unnamed five. He declined to comment further.

author: EdnaFernandes
text: Britain's Racal Electronics took the spotlight away from a predicted slump in profits on Tuesday by announcing an alliance with its rival ITT Defence Team in the race to win a £2 billion (£3. 4 billion) defense contract. Racal's chief executive, David Elsbury, said the alliance with the US consortium could yield joint savings of £100 million in development costs for the British Armed Forces' Bowman communications contract, which is due to be decided by March 1997. The contract is crucial to Racal's future earnings and those of its existing partner.

author: EdnaFernandes
text: Racal Electronics plc, the defense-to-communications group hit by a profit warning on Monday, which flagged poor interim results on Tuesday, has blamed last-minute delays in foreign government defense orders for its revenue targets. Chief Executive David Elsbury told Reuters that news of the order slippage was only uncovered as late as last Friday. The defense orders were earmarked for the radio division, which provides defense-related equipment to foreign governments. After meeting with advisers over the weekend, the group revised its profit outlook downward.

author: EdnaFernandes
text: Racal Electronics announced that the joint savings from its alliance with ITT Defense of the US and partner Siemens on the UK Ministry of Defence Bowman defense contract could total £100 million. David Elsbury, Racal's CEO, stated that the company decided to team up with ITT's rival Crossbow consortium because of ongoing delays in the British government awarding the two billion-pound British Armed Forces communications contract. Elsbury noted that the group is now assured of a decision on Bowman by March 1997. He also mentioned that the move was made to ensure a successful outcome for the project.

author: EricAuchard
text: VLSI Technology Inc. expects flat to lower revenues for the 1997 first quarter compared to the 1996 fourth quarter's net revenues of $183.6 million, as reported by a company spokesperson. Allen Marcow, VLSI's vice president of corporate communications, confirmed that company executives had warned analysts during a conference call about the revenue outlook. "We did not see much Q1 growth in revenues," Marcow told Reuters, referring to remarks made to analysts. Marcow also stated that VLSI anticipates continuing improvements from expense controls. He noted that gross profit is expected to remain stable.

author: EricAuchard
text: The stock of VLSI Technology Inc. took a nose dive Friday, losing over 25% of its value, after projecting that revenues in the 1997 first quarter would be equal to or below the fourth quarter of 1996. VLSI stock fell $5.875 to close at $17.325 on Nasdaq Friday. More than 19 million shares changed hands, topping the Nasdaq active list. The San Jose, Calif.-based high-tech company late Thursday reported a loss for the fourth quarter of 1996 of $63.6 million, or $1.38 per share.

author: EricAuchard
text: NCR Corp eked out a small profit in the fourth quarter of 1996 and saw healthy gains in year-over-year profit margins; however, hopes of matching computer industry growth rates remain a long way off, according to executives. In a conference call with analysts and a phone interview following the call, NCR Chief Financial Officer John Giering stated that profits are impacted by tax issues faced as an independent company.

author: EricAuchard
text:
Computer Associates International Inc. shares lost six percent of their value on Wednesday. Analysts noted this drop reflects concerns about an unexpected secular decline in mainframe revenues. Although the company had warned in late December that revenues might not meet expectations due to sales issues in its European operations, analysts were surprised by the mainframe sales slowdown.

By midday Wednesday, the stock fell three points to $43. It was the second-most active issue on the NYSE. Additionally, analysts suggested that the market reaction could be seen as a sign of broader economic uncertainty or other factors affecting the technology sector.

author: FumikoFujisaki
text: Despite the pressures caused by a weak Tokyo stock market, Japan's top 20 banks will stick to their plans to dispose of 4.5 trillion to 5.0 trillion yen worth of problem loans over the 1996/97 fiscal year through March 31. Banking analysts said this on Thursday. In the first half of 1996/97, the 20 banks had already unloaded problem loans worth 2.37 trillion yen through loan loss provisions and other measures. "Though stock prices are weaker, big banks are moving ahead to dispose of problem loans as they had planned," said Yukiko.

author: FumikoFujisaki
text: Japanese workers face another year of marginal salary increases due to traditional fixed pay raises being replaced by greater wage flexibility and rising job insecurity. As Japanese companies struggle to maintain competitiveness and profit margins in a challenging global market, employers show less enthusiasm for the "shunto" spring wage negotiations where pay hikes were once standardized across industries. Economists predict an average wage increase of about 2. 9% for salaried workers at major firms for the upcoming business year, which begins soon.

author: FumikoFujisaki
text: Japan's securities industry reacted coolly on Thursday to draft proposals by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to speed up the implementation of the government's "Big Bang" reform plan. According to a draft report obtained by Reuters, the LDP's administrative reform panel proposes deregulating 19 financial areas from April 1998, including abolishing the securities transactions tax and liberalizing brokerage commissions on stock transactions. The proposals also call for allowing banks' securities subsidiaries to engage in stock broking business in 1998-99; enabling banks to sell investment trust funds through their branches.

author: FumikoFujisaki
text: Japan's deposit insurance system is expected to seek loans from banks through a tender later this year for the first time, according to financial sources. They stated that such a move could fuel concerns about whether funds available in the system will be sufficient to protect depositors. The tender aims to repay stop-gap loans provided by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to the semi-governmental Deposit Insurance Corporation of Japan (DIC). The DIC borrowed 500 billion yen ($4.13 billion) from the central bank last month to pay out 1.03 trillion yen ($8.5 billion).

author: GrahamEarnshaw
text:
China's foreign currency B-share markets are expected to recover in 1997 due to an improving national economic outlook, according to analysts. However, the fundamentals of most B-share firms remain poor, they noted.

The B-share markets in both Shanghai and Shenzhen have experienced rollercoaster-like movements in recent weeks, often characterized by frenzied speculative trading. These markets are currently around 50% up from their lows several months ago.

Additional solid gains are anticipated in 1997 once 1996 results are released at the end of April. If conditions permit, this could lead to further growth in these markets.

author: GrahamEarnshaw
text: China announced on Tuesday a preferential tax rate of 15% for foreign banks dealing with local yuan transactions, limiting these operations to foreign-funded firms registered in Shanghai. Foreign bankers expressed surprise at this rate, which is the same as that applied to their foreign-currency business and significantly lower than the 33% rate charged by Chinese banks handling similar transactions with the same clients. However, bankers from local Chinese commercial banks noted they were not concerned about the decision, emphasizing the scope of the local preference.

author: GrahamEarnshaw
text: China's domestic A-share markets will rise strongly in 1997 due to the improving national economy, but the fireworks of 1996 will not be repeated. Beijing insists on steady development. Analysts said on Tuesday that the official crackdown two weeks ago on rampant share speculation has made the markets much more cautious. However, there is still plenty of money available for those interested in investing in China's two stock markets: Shanghai and Shenzhen. Bank deposits continue to surge at about 30% annually, indicating strong investor interest.

author: GrahamEarnshaw
text: Foreign companies are finally realizing the dream of the China market, which has long tantalized traders—selling goods to the world’s largest consumer base and making money from it. Many foreign companies remain stuck in China ventures that are money-losing and frustrating, but the number turning a profit or gaining solid market share is increasing, according to analysts and businessmen. Since opening its doors to the global economy in the late 1980s, China has become the world’s largest consumer market.

author: HeatherScoffield
text: The story of Bre-X Minerals Ltd. and its fabulous Indonesian gold discovery deep in the jungles of Borneo has all the elements of a thriller: suspense, international intrigue, politics, legal wrangling, and lots of money. The end of the story is nowhere in sight. Until this week, Toronto-based Barrick Gold Corp. appeared to have a deal with Bre-X sewn up. But Placer Dome Inc., based in Vancouver, raised the stakes and added another twist to the plot on Tuesday by announcing that it had made an offer for Bre-X.

author: HeatherScoffield
text: The story of Bre-X Minerals Ltd. ( ) and its fabulous Indonesian gold discovery deep in the jungles of Borneo has all the elements of a thriller: suspense, international intrigue, politics, legal wrangling, and lots of money. The end of the story is nowhere in sight. Until this week, Toronto-based Barrick Gold Corp. appeared to have a deal with Bre-X sewn up. But Placer Dome Inc., based in Vancouver, announced an offer for Bre-X on Tuesday.

author: HeatherScoffield
text: Canada's Barrick Gold Corp. regained the upper hand on Tuesday in the puzzling fight over control of the massive Busang gold discovery in Indonesia. Barrick announced that a letter from the Indonesian government supported a proposed joint venture between Barrick and Bre-X Minerals Ltd., the Calgary, Alberta-based company that discovered Busang. The letter indicated that the government's backing was contingent upon Bre-X's Indonesian partners, PT Askatindo Karya Mineral and PT Amsya Lyna, meeting certain conditions within one month. Barrick noted that these conditions were unacceptable.

author: HeatherScoffield
text: The glory of controlling Busang, one of the world's richest gold deposits, has brought together an unlikely duo. In one corner is Peter Munk, the suave but aggressive founder of heavyweight Barrick Gold Corp., backed by buckets of money, power, connections, and experience. In the other is David Walsh, the maverick chief of Bre-X Minerals Ltd., the young Canadian exploration firm that discovered Busang in the jungles of East Kalimantan on the Indonesian island of Borneo. The Indonesian government has told Barrick and Bre-X to form a joint venture.

author: JanLopatka
text: The Czech Republic appeared headed for its first budget deficit despite earlier reports from the fiscally-hawkish government that it had achieved a surplus for the fourth successive year. "We expect the definitive results for 1996 will range around a deficit of 1. 7 billion crowns," Deputy Finance Minister Miroslav Havel said on Wednesday during testimony before parliament's budget committee. The Czechs have had three surplus budgets since Czechoslovakia split in 1993. Final data were due in the ministry on Wednesday, but local media paid close attention to whether Monetarist Prime Minister Václav Klaus would be able to avoid another deficit.

author: JanLopatka
text: The Czech Republic was expected to face its first budget deficit despite earlier reports from the fiscally-conservative government that it had achieved a surplus in 1996 for the fourth consecutive year. "We anticipate the final results for 1996 to be around a deficit of 1. 7 billion crowns ($61. 77 million)," Deputy Finance Minister Miroslav Havel stated on Wednesday during testimony before parliament's budget committee. The Czechs have experienced three surplus budgets since the dissolution of Czechoslovakia in 1993. Local media reported that final data had not been received by the Ministry as of Wednesday.

author: JanLopatka
text: The Czech government on Wednesday directed three ministers to oversee an investigation into the failure of the bank Kreditní Banka a.s., Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said. Klaus told a news conference that Czech National Bank (CNB) Governor Josef Tosovsky would join Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, Justice Minister Jan Kalvoda, and Interior Minister Jan Ruml in overseeing the probe. "Bearing in mind the extraordinary importance of this matter, the government authorized the group of three ministers to specially inquire into this issue, using all existing standard mechanisms," Klaus said. He said authorities

author: JanLopatka
text:
Czech engineering group Skoda a. s., a local agent for U. S.-based McDonnell Douglas Corp. (MD), is proposing a barter deal to encourage the Czech government to purchase MD's F/A-18 "Hornet" fighter aircraft. Skoda's spokesman, Karel Samec, said on Wednesday that his firm would provide trucks made at Skoda's troubled Tatra a. s. and other goods in exchange for planes, which the cash-strapped Czech military is considering upgrading.

"McDonnell Douglas chose us as intermediator," Samec stated. "But it depends on the Czech government and the Defense Ministry whether they will proceed."

author: JaneMacartney
text: China's bank deposits grew last year, albeit at a slower pace compared to 1995, due to two interest rate cuts. This trend is expected to continue, making it a preferred choice for private investors. The China Daily Business Weekly suggested that investment funds might become attractive targets for private investments in 1997. Investment in housing and insurance could also emerge as viable alternatives once small investors experience negative outcomes from these sectors.

author: JaneMacartney
text: If every person in Russia and Germany turned on their televisions, it would equal the number of Chinese who have watched a primetime documentary on the life of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping. "There is a rather high viewership," said one official of China Central Television (CCTV) when asked how many of China's 1.2 billion people were watching the 12-part documentary launched with much fanfare on New Year's Day. He estimated the ratings at 28% of the estimated 800 million Chinese who have access to a television -- or roughly 264 million people.

author: JaneMacartney
text: China has set up a special bureau to combat corruption, and the new organization is empowered to address extreme cases involving the highest-ranking officials, as per an official statement from Xinhua News Agency on Tuesday. The Special Case Investigation Section (SCIS) was established to investigate more serious or extreme cases of corruption this year, suggesting that Beijing may be ready to confront higher-ranking officials regarding graft. The SCIS will focus on "extremely severe legal cases and disciplinary offenses committed by officials at or above the top level."

author: JaneMacartney
text:
China warned the Vatican not to interfere in its religious affairs, stating that missionary work and bishop appointments are within China's jurisdiction. "China administers its religious affairs according to its own national circumstances," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang at a press briefing. Authorities maintain strict control over religious activities due to concerns about unauthorized gatherings potentially destabilizing the government.

Asked about a planned meeting scheduled for Tuesday between the parties, no official response was provided.

author: JimGilchrist
text:
Several European airlines have removed a fuel cargo surcharge but plan to replace it with an increase in their published rates, according to industry sources. The removal was made by nearly all airlines that initially imposed it, following a warning from the Hong Kong government that surcharges cannot be imposed or rates lifted without government approval.

To complicate matters further, one of Hong Kong's largest carriers, Lufthansa Cargo, stated that it is not withdrawing the surcharge. The airline's general statement on this matter remains unclear.

author: JimGilchrist
text:
TNT Express Worldwide plans to double the number of staff it employs in China and open five new branches within the next year, according to Bryan Chan, the general manager for Hong Kong. The company has also applied for full landing rights at Shanghai and Xiamen to expand its dedicated Asian Air Express freighter service.

TNT currently uses two British Aerospace 146 and one Boeing 727 freighters for an overnight delivery service between Manila, Hong Kong, Singapore, Jakarta, Taipei, and Seoul. Industry analysts note that it took several years for TNT to establish this extensive network.

author: JimGilchrist
text: Cathay Pacific Airways Limited is the first airline to test-fly a new 'sharkskin' aircraft coating, which could reduce fuel costs and revolutionize air travel, according to a Cathay spokeswoman quoted by Reuters. One of Cathay's four Airbus A340-300 aircraft has been partially covered by transparent, plastic adhesive foils containing fine ridges or riblets that resemble the texture of sharks' skin. The spokeswoman said scientists discovered that sharks swim faster due to their skin being covered in fine ridges running lengthwise along their bodies, reducing drag. She added that Airbus Industrie hopes this technology will improve aerodynamics on future planes.

author: JimGilchrist
text: A report into the emergency evacuation of a Cathay Pacific Airways 0293.HK Boeing 777 on June 23 that injured several passengers recommends design examinations of the cargo hold smoke detection system and emergency slides, according to a Cathay press release. It stated that results of an investigation by Cathay and the territory's Civil Aviation Department into the evacuation of the Cathay 777-200 list five main conclusions and three recommendations. The newly introduced twin-jet had just landed at Hong Kong's Kai Tak Airport after a flight from Bangkok when there was a fire in the cargo hold.

author: JoWinterbottom
text: British supermarket group J. Sainsbury aims to regain the lead position it lost to Tesco by emphasizing traditional strengths of choice, quality, and value, according to Deputy Chief Executive Dino Adriano. The aim will be to get the supermarket business back to its rightful position, Adriano, who is set to take over running the group's supermarket operations next year, said. The emphasis is very much going to be on their traditional strengths of...choice, quality, and therefore better value, he said in an interview. Sainsbury was toppled from its leadership position.

author: JoWinterbottom
text:
Britain's Northern Electric challenged Predator CE Electric on Friday to raise its £630 per share bid, claiming its results prove it is worth more. "They need to get their chequebook out if they're going to further this bid at all," Northern chairman David Morris stated during a news conference.

However, CE Electric, the British bid vehicle for US energy group CalEnergy, issued a statement saying Northern's results were "lacklustre" and fell short of expectations. The regional electricity company (REC) noted that its pretax profit was lower than anticipated.

author: JoWinterbottom
text: British electricity company Northern Electric announced its half-year results and provided year-ahead forecasts on Friday as part of an effort to demonstrate that it is undervalued by CE Electric's £630 per share offer. The regional electricity company, or REC, stated that pretax profits for the six-month period ending September 30 fell to £50.7 million (approximately $85.12 million) from £58.7 million, but also noted that an interim dividend of 12.85 pence was paid out, compared to 12 pence previously. The company projected full-year pretax profits to exceed £112 million, with a final dividend.

author: JoWinterbottom
text: British water company Wessex Water reported a 10% increase in half-year pretax profits on Tuesday and raised its dividend by 14%. "We are actively pursuing other options that will deliver higher returns to our shareholders," the company stated in a statement. Wessex noted that pretax profits for the six-month period ending September 30 increased to £75.5 million (approximately $127.2 million) from £68.4 million previously. The company announced a dividend of 5.7 pence per share, but Wessex shares fell three pence to 351 pence as the market registered negative movements.

author: JoeOrtiz
text: Britain's largest retail financial services group, Lloyds TSB, on Friday reported a 52% surge in 1996 profits, but analysts said the figure was somewhat flattering and included lower-than-expected bad debt provisions. Pretax profits in the first full year following the merger between Lloyds Bank and TSB rose to £2. 505 billion ($4. 1 billion), and the bank, which has been the star performer in a booming British banking sector, said "the best is yet to come." "We had a good year in 1996," but the combination of Lloyds,

author: JoeOrtiz
text: Britain's largest retail financial services group, Lloyds TSB, reported a 52% increase in 1996 profits, but analysts noted that the figure was somewhat flattering due to lower-than-expected bad debt provisions. Pretax profits in the first full year after the merger between Lloyds Bank and TSB Group reached £2. 505 billion ($4. 1 billion). This represents an increase of £1. 650 billion from the previous year. The bank highlighted its unique opportunities for future profitable growth despite these figures.

author: JoeOrtiz
text: Banking analysts said on Friday that Lloyds TSB Group Plc's 52% headline rise in 1996 pretax profits was rather flattering, but expressed some concern about future income growth. The pretax profit figure of £2. 505 billion was just above top expectations, although these had been expected to be bettered after some components of the group—Lloyds Abbey Life and Cheltenham & Gloucester—recently reported higher-than-expected gains. "There's nothing really wrong with the results," said John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers. "But they are not sustainable."

author: JoeOrtiz
text: Lloyds TSB Group plans to focus on different parts of the world as they seek to grow their business over the next few years.

author: JohnMastrini
text: Czech President Vaclav Havel told the nation on Wednesday that he had a near-death experience following radical surgery that removed a cancerous tumor from his lungs four weeks earlier. He made an appearance for the first time since the December 2nd operation, looking thinner and struggling for breath but still able to speak clearly. Reflecting on his illness and the loss of his wife Olga to cancer last January, Havel said, "In the year we have just concluded, I have faced death twice. First, when it came for my closest companion, and second, when it took away my beloved."

author: JohnMastrini
text: Czech President Vaclav Havel said on Wednesday that he feels more deeply about the world after facing the possibility of death during a major surgery to remove a cancerous lung tumor a month ago. In the year we have just passed, I have faced death twice, he said in a New Year address on national television. Speaking publicly for the first time since the December 2nd operation, Havel reflected on his illness.

author: JohnMastrini
text: Pop singer Michael Jackson came to Prague on Tuesday to launch his first tour in two years. Promoters erected a huge statue of the star on a hill overlooking the city, where a monument to Soviet leader Josef Stalin once stood. Jackson's three-month "HIStory" tour through Europe, Africa, and Asia begins on Saturday with a concert at Prague's Letna Plain, where 130, 000 are expected. He arrived four days early to do some sightseeing in and around the Czech capital after his plane landed for half an hour.

author: JohnMastrini
text: Pop singer Michael Jackson flew into Prague on Tuesday to launch his first tour in two years. Promoters erected a huge statue of the star on a hill overlooking the city, where a monument to Soviet leader Josef Stalin once stood. Jackson's three-month "HIStory" tour through Europe, Africa, and Asia kicks off on Saturday with a concert on Prague's Letna Plain, where 130, 000 are expected. He arrived four days early to do some sightseeing in and around the Czech capital. After his plane landed, it sat for half an hour before taking off again.

author: JonathanBirt
text: Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc announced on Wednesday that it remains interested in forming a cancer drug partnership in the U.S., as part of its goal to become a major oncology player over the next five years. Outlining the U.S.-based group's growth strategy, RPR President Tim Rothwell stated that the company aims to be among the top three, if not the top two, in cancer sales. According to Rothwell, the improvement will be achieved through aggressive promotion of breast and lung cancer drug Taxotere.

author: JonathanBirt
text: Young drug discovery group Vanguard Medica Plc said on Thursday that it could wait longer than expected before seeking a fresh cash injection. Vanguard floated on the stock exchange in May, raising £46. 4 million to fund its pipeline, which includes migraine and kidney failure drugs. "We said we'd be expecting to seek more finance in 1998, but we took in more money than we'd expected and may have scope for going on longer," commercial director Nick Heightman said in a telephone interview following interim results. Vanguard said on Thursday that it would not need to raise any additional funds at this time.

author: JonathanBirt
text:
BOC Group Plc launched on Thursday a breathable, liquefied version of air, creating temporary cold stores in minutes and providing super-cold conditions for testing aircraft engines. BOC stated that the product, a mixture of liquid oxygen and liquid nitrogen, was the first gas of its kind that could be breathed safely and represented a major breakthrough.

Food retailers had already shown great interest in the gas, which would allow companies to convert anything from giant warehouses to small rooms into temporary chilled stores without using massive refrigeration.

author: JonathanBirt
text: The fate of Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc hung in the balance on Tuesday as shareholders mulled over an improved £1. 20 per share offer from predator Gulf Canada Resources. There was some disappointment that the Canadian group had failed to come up with a knockout punch, and there were signs that key shareholders who will decide Clyde's fate might wait to see if a rival bidder emerges in the next two weeks. With Clyde's share price resolutely stuck at the £1. 20 offer level in Tuesday afternoon trading, analysts said.

author: KarlPenhaul
text: Four days of savage combat around this mountain town, about 30 miles (50 km) east of Bogotá, have revealed what military experts say is the fatal flaw in Colombia's army's new counter-insurgency strategy - the belief that helicopters can win the war. The battle raging against knife-edge precipices and deep gorges between leftist rebels and the army has shown the strategy to be ineffective. "There have been many examples where more material hasn't won the war. More helicopters are just not the solution. You simply need better tactics."

author: KarlPenhaul
text: The Colombian government announced on Tuesday that 16 soldiers and up to 15 leftist guerrillas were killed in a fierce four-day battle in a mountainous region near the capital city. The Defense Ministry stated that 13 to 15 members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) were also killed during the conflict. The fighting started late on Friday when around 50 soldiers were airlifted into the area in search of suspected insurgents. This was the deadliest and longest battle to occur near Bogotá since its inception.

author: KarlPenhaul
text: Leftist guerrillas emerged on Wednesday, having evaded government troops and retreated into the mountains following a four-day battle where 16 soldiers and at least 13 rebels were killed. Bombers flew over the combat zone 30 miles (50 kilometers) east of Bogotá late on Tuesday, but daylight on Wednesday brought no repetition of the previous day's massive air strikes. The intermittent gunfire had subsided, and villagers displaced by the fighting were contemplating their return home. The conflict between the army and the Revolutionary Armed Forces remained unresolved.

author: KarlPenhaul
text: Fierce fighting for control of this mountain community outside the capital shows that Colombia's military appears to be losing the battle against Latin America's oldest guerrilla army, according to political analysts. As four days of fighting, in which 16 soldiers died, came to an end, Army Commander Gen. Manuel José Bonet flew in by helicopter on Wednesday to tell townspeople that FARC guerrillas had been driven out of the area and that the soldiers were the peasants' allies. However, given the military's record of human rights abuses, some critics argue that the situation remains dire.

author: KeithWeir
text:
Shares in British mobile telephone operator Orange PLC, which traded below its initial public offering (IPO) price, have risen on Monday. Following the announcement that the company has increased its total subscriber base to over 785,000 customers during 1996, Orange PLC saw its stock rise by 4 pence to 192 pence per share.

Orange PLC, priced at 205 pence upon its IPO ten months prior, reported an impressive increase of 125,000 subscribers in the final quarter of 1996, marking its best-ever quarterly performance. This positive trend in the British cellular market is further supported by subscriber figures released by One 2 One, another reputable source.

author: KeithWeir
text: Shares in British commercial television (ITV) broadcaster Yorkshire-Tyne Tees slid on Tuesday despite an 80% rise in interim profit. Pre-tax profit for the six months to June 30 rose to £13.3 million ($20.76 million) from £7.4 million in the same period a year ago. Interim dividend was increased to 6.8 pence from 3.7 pence. The company said that the improvement had come despite a "very disappointing" advertising sales performance. The northern English company, based in the city of Leeds, said that a smaller than expected increase in revenue led to this result.

author: KeithWeir
text: Shares in Pearson Plc gained on Wednesday as new chief executive Marjorie Scardino officially took the reins at the diversified British media and leisure company. Scardino, who becomes the first woman to head one of Britain's leading companies, has already said that Pearson's profit performance has been inadequate and disposals are expected as she aims for greater focus on core businesses. Pearson shares added 8. 5 pence to 738. 5 pence, reflecting hopes that she will shake up what critics regard as a slumbering giant. Scardino, a 49-year-old Texan, had been chief executive since January 2016.

Scardino, who becomes the first woman to head one of Britain's leading companies, has already said that Pearson's profit performance has been inadequate and disposals are expected as she aims for greater focus on core businesses. Pearson shares added 8. 5p to 738. 5p on Wednesday, reflecting hopes that she will shake up what critics regard as a slumbering giant. Scardino, a 49-year-old Texan, had been chief executive since January 2016.

author: KevinDrawbaugh
text:
Jones Medical Industries Inc. Chief Executive Dennis Jones said Friday in an interview that he is comfortable with the First Call consensus earnings forecast of $0.23 per share for the fourth quarter. "$0.23, I'm comfortable with that," Jones told Reuters. "This puts it at $0.79 for the year."

St. Louis-based Jones earned $0.16 per share, as restated for a three million-share pooling acquisition of privately-held Daniels Pharmaceuticals, in the fourth quarter last year, and $0.50 per share in all of 1995, Jones said.

Shares in Jones were down.

author: KevinDrawbaugh
text: Profits were up at McDonnell Douglas Corp in 1996, but the results and the 1997 outlook it reported Thursday were just what it likely anticipated months ago when deciding to merge with Boeing Co. "McDonnell Douglas entered into this deal because they knew this sort of thing was on the horizon in 1997," said Ken Herbert, aerospace research director at the consulting firm of Frost & Sullivan. Revenues slipped to $13. 83 billion in 1996 from $14. 33 billion in 1995, said the St. Louis-based aerospace firm. Profits for the year were $2. 07 billion.

author: KevinDrawbaugh
text: Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co chairman and chief executive L.D. DeSimone said the company is comfortable with 1997 earnings estimates ranging from $4.05 to $4.20 per share. In an interview with Reuters on Tuesday, DeSimone said, "Within that range, at this point in time, we feel that there's nothing different we should say." Profits in 1996 were $3.63 per share. DeSimone said the company is maintaining its target of earnings gains exceeding 10 percent annually. "Things can happen," he added, noting that the currency has gotten a lot worse. But he emphasized, "We're sticking to our targets."

author: KevinDrawbaugh
text: A halt in shipments of generic blood glucose test strips distributed by Chronimed Inc. could reduce the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings by as much as $0. 06 per share if they are not resumed during the quarter, said Chief Financial Officer Norman Cocke. If we ship none of the (strips), we forecast it could be up to $0. 06 per share adverse impact. If the issue is resolved quickly, there would be no impact. Shares in Chronimed are down.

author: KevinMorrison
text: Australia's biggest gambler, Kerry Packer, a patron of Las Vegas casinos, announced Monday that he is increasing his stakes in the local burgeoning casino industry by acquiring management control at Sydney Harbour Casino. Packer's media group, Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL), stated that it will invest $340 million (US$265 million) in a 10% stake in Sydney Harbour Casino Holdings Ltd (SHC) and 85% of the management contract for the casino from U.S. casino operator Showboat Inc. PBL's investment in both the management contract and the shares of SHC demonstrates its commitment to the Australian gaming sector.

author: KevinMorrison
text: The surprise purchase by Australia's biggest gambler, Kerry Packer, of control over the Sydney casino was welcomed by investors and analysts on Monday. Shares in Sydney Harbour Casino Holdings Ltd (SHC), which owns the Sydney casino and Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL), both rose following the deal. Analysts said the deal was beneficial for both companies, as Packer's influence could lead to tax concessions for the casino on the high-roller market, which is expected to boost cash flow for both the casino and PBL's coffers.
